model.label: Statutory social health insurance through competing sickness funds, with an opt-out private tier

overview.statement: In 2024 about 89% of residents were covered by statutory health insurance and about 10% by substitutive private insurance; roughly 0.1% had no coverage.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

overview.statement: Statutory coverage is provided through 96 competing, not-for-profit sickness funds.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

overview.statement: A self-governing body of payers and providers, the Federal Joint Committee (G-BA), decides which technologies, medicines and devices the statutory benefit package covers and sets care standards.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

financing.statement: Statutory insurance is funded mainly by payroll contributions: a general rate of 14.6% of gross wages plus a fund-specific supplementary rate, both split equally between employer and employee. Contributions are pooled in a central health fund and passed to sickness funds using risk adjustment.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

financing.statement: The health ministry set the average supplementary contribution for 2027 at 2.9%, unchanged from 2026; each sickness fund still sets its own rate.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

financing.statement: Employees above an income threshold (EUR 73,800 a year), the self-employed and civil servants may choose private insurance instead of the statutory system.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

financing.statement: Private insurance premiums are set by age and health risk, whereas statutory contributions depend on income.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

financing.statement: Mandatory long-term care insurance, introduced in 1994, covers almost the entire population, with contributions split between members and employers.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

covered.statement: The statutory benefit package is broad and identical for every insured person, going beyond essential services; substitutive private plans usually match or exceed it.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

covered.statement: Patients can choose their own GP, specialists, dentists and pharmacies; GPs are usually the first contact but do not formally control referrals.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

covered.statement: Since 2004 sickness funds have had to offer an optional GP-centred care model, and some reward members who follow it.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

covered.statement: Germany reimburses about 90% of authorised medicines, against an EU average of 43%, and new medicines reach reimbursement in an average of 128 days versus 578 across the EU.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

cost_sharing.statement: Out-of-pocket payments made up 11% of health spending in 2023, below the EU average of 16%.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

cost_sharing.statement: Outpatient prescriptions carry a 10% co-payment of at least EUR 5 and at most EUR 10; under-18s are exempt.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

cost_sharing.statement: Annual co-payments are capped relative to income, but patients must apply to benefit from the cap.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

cost_sharing.statement: Dental care involves explicit cost sharing and is not fully covered by statutory insurance.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

cost_sharing.statement: Because long-term care insurance covers costs only partially, long-term care accounts for 38% of all out-of-pocket health spending.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

additional_care.statement: Voluntary private insurance pays for about 3% of health spending, mostly to top up areas the statutory package only partly covers, such as dental care.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

additional_care.statement: 52 private insurance companies offer substitutive and supplementary cover.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

access.statement: In 2024 only 1.2% of people reported an unmet need for a medical examination, compared with an EU average of 3.6%.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

access.statement: Unmet need for dental care was 0.9%, against an EU average of 6.3%.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

access.statement: Reported unmet need for mental health care rose from 4% in 2021 to 10% in 2024, and there is a shortage of outpatient psychotherapists.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

access.statement: Around 15% of people cannot reach an emergency department within 15 minutes by car, but almost everyone can within 30 minutes.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

access.statement: Germany had 4.7 practising physicians and 12.3 nurses per 1,000 people in 2023 (EU nurse average 8.5); GPs make up about 16% of doctors, below the 20% average across 24 EU countries.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

access.statement: Staff shortages persist in hospitals and long-term care, and nurse-to-bed ratios are relatively low.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth was 81.5 years in 2024, 0.2 years below the EU average.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

outcomes.statement: Between 2010 and 2019 life expectancy rose by 0.8 years, about half the EU-wide gain of 1.5 years.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

outcomes.statement: In 2022 treatable mortality was 83 per 100,000 (EU 90) and preventable mortality 165 per 100,000, slightly below the EU average.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

outcomes.statement: 30-day mortality after a heart attack was 8.6% in 2021, higher than in Denmark (4.8%) and other neighbouring countries.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

outcomes.statement: Insurance claims data from one large German insurer show the life-expectancy gap between low- and high-income groups widening among older men, while narrowing slightly among women.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

costs.statement: Germany spent 11.7% of GDP on health in 2023 (EU 10.0%), EUR 5,414 per person adjusted for purchasing power, the highest in the EU.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

costs.statement: Public sources fund 86% of health spending, above the EU average of 80%.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

costs.statement: Retail spending on medicines was EUR 743 per person in 2023, the highest in the EU (average EUR 510), and about 14% of total health spending.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

costs.statement: Statutory insurance spending was expected to grow by almost 7% in 2026 and by less than 3% in 2027.

what_works.statement: The European Observatory lists universal coverage, a comprehensive benefit package, low cost-sharing, free choice of provider and short waiting times among the system's strengths.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

what_works.statement: People at risk of poverty report very little unmet medical need: 1.7% in 2024, against 6.0% for the same group across the EU.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

what_works.statement: Generics account for 84% of prescription volume, the highest share in the EU, though the share has stopped growing.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

problems.statement: In a 2025 survey of 2,201 adults, only about 20% believed statutory and privately insured patients receive the same quality of care, and close to 80% favoured abolishing the separate private tier, a majority in every political group.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

problems.statement: Outpatient and hospital care are organised and paid for separately, which fragments care; despite hospitals offering more outpatient services, there are few structural incentives for integration.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

problems.statement: Hospital capacity is very high, 7.7 beds per 1,000 people in 2023 against an EU average of 5.1, alongside many avoidable admissions for chronic conditions.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

problems.statement: The Observatory flags concerns about oversupply and efficiency, and a complex, self-governing stewardship structure that tends to produce only incremental change.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

problems.statement: Digitalisation is uneven and electronic health records are little used: only 5.1% of people accessed records online in 2024.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

reforms.statement: A 2026 contribution-stabilisation law (GKV-BStabG) is expected to relieve sickness funds by up to EUR 19 billion in 2027, and a government finance commission is due to propose structural reforms by the end of 2026.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

reforms.statement: A hospital reform in force since January 2025 has states assign hospitals to defined service groups, adds standby (provision) payments alongside per-case DRG payments, shifts care to outpatient settings and creates intersectoral facilities, backed by a EUR 50 billion transformation fund for 2026-2035.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

reforms.statement: The nationwide rollout of an electronic patient record for the statutorily insured began in April 2025, after pilot regions.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

reforms.statement: Hybrid DRG payments for selected procedures that can be done as inpatient or outpatient care began in 2024; their impact is expected to stay small for several years.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

us_lessons.statement: Comparing the US with ten high-income countries including Germany (data mostly 2013-2016), researchers found the US spent roughly twice as much while using care at similar rates; prices of labour and goods, including medicines, and administrative costs drove the difference.

verification.note: Researched from the source text; awaiting fetch-and-fingerprint run.

us_lessons.statement: Administrative costs were 8% of US health spending, against 1% to 3% in the comparison countries, which include Germany.
